claim_a.quote: Our CRM shows customer churn running at 19%, which is exactly why we need to get more aggressive on price before we bleed out.

claim_b.quote: Net revenue attrition was eight and a half percent last year. Nowhere near the number Dale keeps quoting in leadership meetings.

resolution: Both numbers are real but measure different things. The CRM lapse_90d flag counts ANY 90-day order gap (19.3% in FY2025), sweeping in seasonal K-12 accounts every summer and street accounts that skip a quarter. True 12-month account attrition is 11.2%; because churned accounts average 58% of median size, net revenue attrition is 8.5%. The planning figure is 8.5%.
why_decidable: The controller's memo walks the reconciliation line by line (19.3% -> 11.2% -> 8.5%) and states which definition finance uses for planning; the CRM data dictionary confirms lapse_90d is a flag, not an attrition rate.

claim_a.quote: The chain business is our growth engine. We have grown it 38% in two years and it is profitable growth — every case we ship a chain is a case our competitors don't.

claim_b.quote: Once you load in delivery cost, the chain book earns us less than a point of contribution margin. We are running trucks for practice.

resolution: Chain revenue did grow 38.4% (92.8 -> 128.4) but at 12.2% GM with 11.3% delivery cost-to-serve (41,600 drops x $349 = $14.5M), contribution margin is ~0.9%. Chain growth is near-zero-profit growth; the claim of 'profitable growth' is false at the contribution line.
why_decidable: Both CSVs are internal finance/ops data with row-level figures; the arithmetic (12.2% - 11.3% = 0.9%) is mechanical once the two files are joined.

claim_a.quote: Price is number one, two, and three with these customers. Everything else is decoration.

resolution: The n=412 customer survey ranks price 4th of 7 switching drivers (weighted score 6.8), behind order accuracy & fill rate (8.4), delivery reliability & windows (8.1), and rep category support (7.2). Rep anecdote reflects negotiation salience, not switching behavior.
why_decidable: Structured survey of 412 customers beats single-rep anecdote; the customer panel transcript independently corroborates service-driven switching stories.

claim_a.quote: we proudly serve more than 3,100 customers across four states

resolution: The CRM holds 3,109 account records, of which 495 are dormant (no order in trailing 365 days). Active accounts = 2,614. The 3,100 figure counts dormant records; marketing copy and Tyler's slack reuse it.
why_decidable: The data dictionary defines 'active' precisely and states the split (3,109 = 2,614 active + 495 dormant) as of 2026-05-31.

claim_a.quote: over half our street customers are already ordering online anyway, this portal push is a solution looking for a problem

claim_b.quote: portal_enrolled = Y on 492 of 1,588 active street accounts (31.0%) as of 2026-05-31

resolution: Actual street portal adoption is 31.0%, less than half the peer median of 65%. Dale's 'over half' is wrong even counting enrollment generously; portal-enrolled accounts place only ~64% of their orders via portal.
why_decidable: Field-level CRM count vs an unsourced slack assertion; portal_order_analytics_fy2025.csv corroborates (29,500 of 148,200 street orders via portal).

claim_a.quote: fwiw i pulled some benchmark numbers and peer private label penetration is like 10%, so at 9% were basically at market. not much upside there imo

claim_b.quote: Median private-label penetration among regional broadline distributors in the $250M-$1B revenue cohort was 19.6% of sales in FY2024, with an interquartile range of 18-22%.

resolution: Tyler pulled the wrong cohort row — the study's exhibit also lists convenience-channel distributors at 10.4%, which is not Bluestem's peer set. The correct benchmark is 18-22%; Bluestem's 9.0% implies a large, real PL upside (~$1.8M GP at 15% penetration).
why_decidable: The study explicitly scopes each cohort and the exhibit table labels the 10.4% row 'convenience-channel distributors'; Bluestem is squarely in the $250M-$1B broadline cohort.

topic: Why Bluestem lost the Heartland GPO award

claim_a.quote: We lost the Heartland GPO award on price, plain and simple. It will keep happening until we sharpen pencils.

claim_b.quote: Your pricing was within 1.5% of the awarded distributor. The award decision was driven by service commitments: the awarded distributor guaranteed a 98.5% fill rate and twice-weekly delivery to our rural facilities.

resolution: Heartland's own written debrief says the loss was on service levels, not price — Bluestem's healthcare fill rate was 94.1% at bid time vs the required 98.5%. The demand-recovery initiative is a service/fill-rate investment ahead of the spring 2027 rebid, not a price move.
why_decidable: The customer's debrief is first-party and quantified; the ops memo independently confirms the 94.1% fill rate and costs the fix (~$1.4M).

topic: Food show ROI: $3.2M pipeline vs $241K attributable

claim_a.quote: the show generated $3.2M in qualified pipeline

claim_b.quote: campaign_source was populated on 6.3% of post-show orders. Orders we can actually attribute to the April show total $241K.

resolution: The $3.2M is a self-reported sum of lead sheets, not tracked conversions. Attribution is broken (6.3% field fill), so true ROI on the $410K show is unknown but demonstrably far below the claimed pipeline. The initiative is to fix attribution and reallocate, not to take the pipeline number at face value.
why_decidable: The controller's pull is field-level CRM data; Gwen's recap itself concedes in passing that leads are 'self-reported at the booth'.

topic: What the Springfield price pilot proved

claim_a.quote: When we tested sharper pricing in Springfield, volume responded immediately — proof that price moves the needle.

claim_b.quote: Volume moved less than two percent and we gave up almost nine percent of gross profit dollars in that cohort. If that's the needle moving, it moved the wrong way.

resolution: The pilot CSV shows a 3.0% list cut (2.6% realized) produced only +1.8% case volume (elasticity ~-0.7) and -8.8% GP dollars vs control. The pilot refutes, not supports, an across-the-board price cut.
why_decidable: Row-level pilot-vs-control data with month-by-month volume and GP; Dale's memo cites no numbers.
